To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
biliary proteins in gallstones from patients with cholesterol crystals and calcium phosphate were different from those in gallstones without crystals and calcium phosphate.

1) the biliary proteins in gallstone patients are not significantly different from those in patients without stones; 2) the biliary protein concentrations are significantly different in patients with and without gallstones; 3) biliary protein concentrations in patients with gallstones are significantly higher than in patients without gallstones; and 4) the biliary concentrations of albumin, transferrin and IgG are significantly higher in patients with gallstone disease than in those without stones.
biliary proteins in the gallbladder of patients with and without gallstones differ.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the biliary proteins in patients with and without gallstones.
the study of proteins in the biliary system.

the development of new methods for the detection of proteins in biological fluids, and the application of these methods to the study of the proteins of bile, with particular reference to their relationship to the pathogenesis of cholesterol gallstones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gallbladder and bile ducts are the most likely sites of origin of gallbladder cancer.

the gallbladder mucosa in patients with gallstones has a higher concentration of biliary proteins than that of normal patients, and this difference is more pronounced in the patients with gallstones who have had symptoms of biliary tract disease.
there is no evidence that biliary proteins have any role in gallstone formation, but there is evidence that the proteins are not without function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
biliary proteins are altered in the presence of gallstones.
biliary proteins are not a major factor in gallstone formation and that they do not have a role in the pathogenesis of cholesterol gallstones.
we are trying to understand the mechanisms of gallstone formation and to identify novel targets for therapy.

biliary proteins are not only present but are actually more abundant in gallstone patients than in non-gallstone patients.
we can use a combination of proteomics and metabolomics to identify proteins and metabolites that are associated with the presence of gallstones.
